title: Stasimon 3 (lines 1103–1114)

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus joyfully guesses that Oedipus was born on Mount Cithaeron, perhaps the child of a mountain nymph and a god: Pan, Loxias (Apollo), Cyllene’s lord or Bacchus.

context.history: Greek myths often told of heroes fathered by gods on mountains.

significance: This brief, happy ode is placed just before the worst discovery, a classic tragic moment of false hope
discussionQuestions: Why might a writer put a happy moment just before a disaster?
Where does irony appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with pride and fall?

In Stasimon 1 the Chorus refused to accept the seer's charge and remembered how Oedipus proved true like gold. In Stasimon 3 it again chooses the most generous reading of the facts, turning a foundling's story into a tale of divine birth. In both odes, loyalty to the king shapes how the elders read the evidence.

items.prompt: Analyze the dramatic irony of Stasimon 3 as a whole.
items.expected: The Chorus celebrates a birth it believes will prove glorious, imagining Pan or Loxias as the father. But the audience has heard Jocasta's story of an infant cast away on the mountain with pinned ankles and has just watched her leave in horror. The joyful guesses therefore sound hollow, and the ode's hope becomes a measure of how far the elders are from the truth.

satQuestions.passage:
If my soul prophetic err not, if my wisdom aught avail,
Thee, Cithaeron, I shall hail,
As the nurse and foster-mother of our Oedipus shall greet
Ere tomorrow’s full moon rises, and exalt thee as is meet.
Dance and song shall hymn thy praises, lover of our royal race.
Phoebus, may my words find grace!
Child, who bare thee, nymph or goddess? sure sire was more than man,
Haply the hill-roamer Pan.
Or did Loxias beget thee, for he haunts the upland wold;
Or Cyllene’s lord, or Bacchus, dweller on the hilltops cold?
Did some Heliconian Oread give him thee, a new-born joy?
Nymphs with whom he loves to toy?

weDoAnswers: Greek myths often told of heroes fathered by gods on mountains. Read closely: “Dance and song shall hymn thy praises, lover of our royal race.” (Chorus, lines 1107).
analysis.weDoWords: “Dance”, “hymn” and “royal race” stand out. The elders imagine celebrating Cithaeron for nursing a royal child, and their joy makes the truth that follows more painful.

segments.script: Greek myths often told of heroes fathered by gods on mountains. This brief, happy ode is placed just before the worst discovery, a classic tragic moment of false hope Irony: The Chorus celebrates Mount Cithaeron and imagines a divine father for Oedipus at the very moment the inquiry is about to answer the question of his birth. Tone / mood: The ode is brief, excited and hopeful: the elders promise dances and songs and picture Oedipus as the child of a god and a mountain nymph. Allusion: The elders list gods of the wild who might have fathered a child on the mountain (Pan, Loxias, Cyllene’s lord and Bacchus), alluding to myths of heroes born of gods. Watch for Mount Cithaeron: The mountain where the infant was found becomes, in the elders' song, a place of divine birth and celebration.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
